title: Ripe Fruit and Rigged Scales
overview: Amos sees a basket of late summer fruit as a sign that Israel's time is up, and he names the cheating of the poor that has brought it to this point.

parts.label: The basket of fruit (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: In Hebrew the word for summer fruit sounds almost like the word for "end," so the basket is a pun: Israel is ripe, and its end has come. The temple songs, probably at Israel's royal shrine at Bethel, will turn to wailing, with so many dead that bodies are thrown out in silence and no one mourns them properly.

parts.label: Cheating the poor (vv. 4-6)
parts.note: Trading was banned on the monthly new moon feast and the weekly Sabbath, and these merchants can hardly wait to sell again with short measures, rigged weights and grain padded with sweepings. Buying needy people for silver or the price of cheap footwear points to people forced into slavery over tiny debts.

parts.label: An oath that will not be forgotten (vv. 7-8)
parts.note: The LORD swears by the thing Jacob's people take pride in, and scholars are unsure whether this means God himself, Israel's temple and privileges, or, with bitter irony, Israel's own arrogance. The land heaving and sinking like the yearly flooding of the Nile may picture an earthquake or simply total upheaval.

parts.label: Darkness and mourning (vv. 9-10)
parts.note: The sun going down at noon is an image of sudden disaster, and some scholars link it to a solar eclipse of that era. Rough sackcloth and shaved heads were signs of grief, and mourning an only son was the deepest loss people could imagine.

parts.label: A famine of God's word (vv. 11-12)
parts.note: The people who told Amos to stop prophesying (chapter 7) will one day search everywhere for a word from God and find none. They will roam from sea to sea and from north to east, possibly never thinking to look south toward Jerusalem.

parts.label: False oaths will fail (vv. 13-14)
parts.note: Even the strongest young people will faint, and those who swear by "the sin of Samaria," by Dan's god and by the shrine at Beersheba will fall for good. Dan and Beersheba sat at the far north and south of the land, and the sin of Samaria probably means an idol such as the golden calf images, though the exact meaning of these phrases is debated.

think: When people quietly bend the rules to profit from those with less, what do you think that slowly does to a whole community?
